title: Hermeneutics (the theory of interpretation)
body: Hermeneutics (the theory of interpretation) — an engine domain that can touch it: philosophy. Calibration: map-only — out of scope for sealing — foundational, empirical or interpretive (RESONANCE); for theology, CONCORDANT: a signpost, never HOLDS. How meaning is drawn from a text, and what makes one reading better than another. THE HERMENEUTICAL CIRCLE is its central finding: the parts are understood through the whole and the whole through the parts, so understanding is necessarily iterative — you arrive with a pre-understanding, the text corrects it, and you read again with the corrected one. THE SCHOOLS DISAGREE AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS KEPT: Alexandria (Origen) read allegorically for a spiritual sense beneath the letter, Antioch (Theodore, Chrysostom) held to the literal-historical sense; the Reformers held perspicuity and the grammatical-historical method — the text means what its author meant, in its language and its moment — against a reading secured by magisterium; the historical-critical school treats pre-understanding as contamination to be removed, while Gadamer answers that it is the very condition of understanding, and calls the goal a fusion of horizons. Ricoeur adds the hermeneutic of suspicion: ask what a text conceals as well as what it says. WHY IT BINDS HERE: every rule this library runs on is a hermeneutical commitment — original languages carry the authority, translation is a vehicle, a citation is not a proof, and authority is never silently upgraded by saving, repeating or hashing a claim. Kept as map-only: which reading is right is not a computation, and a tool that sealed an interpretation would be doing the reader's work and calling it verification.

interpretation presupposes signs that mean at all; Peirce's interpretant -- the effect in a mind that takes something AS a sign -- puts interpretation inside the sign's own structure, which is where hermeneutics begins
a reading is argued: it draws inferences from the text and from context, and the standards for a good inference are logic's

grammar does not determine meaning. The same well-formed sentence means differently in different mouths and moments -- irony, genre, and the speaker's situation decide what syntax leaves open -- so a complete account of competence still cannot deliver the sense of an utterance. This is the honest boundary between the two, and it runs in this direction

the hermeneutical circle IS iterative conditioning: pre-understanding is a prior, the text is evidence, the revised understanding is a posterior, and you read again with it as the new prior. Gadamer's fusion of horizons and Bayesian updating are the same shape -- which is also why neither can start from nowhere: a flat prior is still a prior, and a reading with no pre-understanding is not a purer reading but an unexamined one
you cannot interpret what you have not first established: for any ancient work the reading itself is reconstructed from disagreeing copies, so exegesis stands on the apparatus

title: Textual criticism (establishing what the text says)
body: Textual criticism (establishing what the text says) — an engine domain that can touch it: linguistics. Calibration: map-only — out of scope for sealing — foundational, empirical or interpretive (RESONANCE); for theology, CONCORDANT: a signpost, never HOLDS. Before what a text MEANS there is what it SAYS, and for any ancient work that is recovered rather than given: no autograph survives, so the reading is reconstructed from copies that disagree. The craft weighs manuscripts by age, family and geography, and applies canons a scribe's habits make sensible — prefer the harder reading (a copyist smooths difficulty, he does not manufacture it) and the shorter (glosses accrete). THE SCHOOLS DISAGREE: reasoned eclecticism weighs internal and external evidence case by case; the Byzantine-priority view holds that the majority of witnesses preserves the text; Westcott-Hort privileged the Alexandrian family. The disagreement is real, the stakes are usually small, and both facts belong on the card. WHY IT BINDS HERE: this library anchors bodies by sha256 and cuts cards at byte offsets so a passage can be re-read from the source — which is textual criticism's discipline in machine form, applied to our own copies.

title: Translation theory (formal vs dynamic equivalence)
body: Translation theory (formal vs dynamic equivalence) — an engine domain that can touch it: linguistics. Calibration: map-only — out of scope for sealing — foundational, empirical or interpretive (RESONANCE); for theology, CONCORDANT: a signpost, never HOLDS. No two languages cut the world at the same joints, so every translation trades something. FORMAL EQUIVALENCE follows the source's words and structure and asks the reader to travel; DYNAMIC (functional) equivalence, named by Eugene Nida, follows the source's EFFECT and brings the meaning to the reader. Neither is neutral and neither is dishonest: a wooden rendering can obscure sense, and a fluent one can quietly decide an ambiguity the original left open. Untranslatables are the proof — Hebrew *hesed*, Greek *logos*, *charis* — where any single English word is already an interpretation. WHY IT BINDS HERE: this library treats the original tongues as the authority and a translation as a vehicle, which is a translation-theoretic position, not a neutral default — so the word-study path shows the Hebrew or Greek beneath the English rather than asking the reader to trust the rendering.

title: Semiotics (sign, signified, interpretant)
body: Semiotics (sign, signified, interpretant) — an engine domain that can touch it: linguistics. Calibration: map-only — out of scope for sealing — foundational, empirical or interpretive (RESONANCE); for theology, CONCORDANT: a signpost, never HOLDS. The general theory of signs — how anything stands for anything else. Saussure gave the dyad (signifier/signified) and the finding that the link is ARBITRARY: nothing about the sound 'tree' resembles a tree, so meaning is carried by difference within a system rather than by resemblance. Peirce gave the triad — sign, object, and INTERPRETANT, the effect in a mind that takes it as a sign — which makes interpretation part of the sign's own structure rather than something added afterwards, and connects semiotics to hermeneutics at the root. His icon/index/symbol division is still the working taxonomy: smoke is an index of fire, a portrait an icon of a face, a word a symbol by convention. WHY IT BINDS HERE: a card is a sign standing for a source, and the project's whole discipline is refusing to let the sign be mistaken for the thing — a fingerprint is not a verdict, a citation is not a proof.
